verification.note: Code facts reproduced by reading. VolumeSlider.tsx:73 is the only pointer handler on the input (`onPointerUp={(e) => releasePointerFocus(e.currentTarget)}`); there is no onPointerDown, setPointerCapture or onBlur. SeekBar.tsx:141-142 calls setPointerCapture on pointerdown, SeekBar.tsx:155-158 blurs on pointerup, and the comment at 162-164 names a pointer released outside the input as a case to handle. The e2e volume test (controls-autohide-focus-desktop.spec.ts:28-31, 65-74) uses page.mouse.click at the centre of the slider, so a drag released outside the 80px (w-20, VolumeSlider.tsx:47) input is never exercised. The claim is about dependence, not a proven failure: a native range thumb drag usually captures mouse events internally in Blink and Gecko, which would route the pointerup to the input. I could not run a browser, so whether focus actually stays on the slider after an outside release is unproven. If it does stay, the input keeps focus and the next key press makes it :focus-visible, which holds the bar on screen through has-[:focus-visible] (PointerControlsPresenter.tsx:95). That is the exact symptom this change fixes.

unspecified_scores.reason: After a mouse click on a control, a Tab press is affected only if the browser resets its sequential-focus starting point on blur(). Chromium usually keeps the click point as the starting point, so at most the user sees Tab land on an earlier element than expected, and this needs mixed mouse and Tab use.
It needs a screen reader activation that dispatches a click with detail > 0. The single home user is not described as using assistive technology, and the only result is focus moving to the body.
A touch tap on the seek bar or a shared ControlButton blurs it. Touch focus rarely becomes :focus-visible and there is no keyboard to continue from, so the user sees no difference.

specification_compliance: The change follows the stated aim in pointerFocus.ts:1-6: a control pressed with the pointer drops focus, and one reached from the keyboard keeps it. ControlButton tells the two apart by click detail (ControlButton.tsx:55-56). The sliders blur on pointerup (SeekBar.tsx:157, VolumeSlider.tsx:73).
Unlike SeekBar, VolumeSlider does not capture the pointer, so releasing a drag outside the input depends on how the browser routes native range drags (CR-2).

potential_unspecified_behavior.behavior: Before this change, after a mouse click on the volume slider, the focused INPUT took ArrowUp/ArrowDown and changed the volume natively, because ShortcutsProvider.tsx:74-79 treats an INPUT target as editing and skips the video shortcuts. Now focus goes to the body, so the same key press runs the global video shortcuts in useVideoShortcuts.ts:46-63 and seeks ±60s instead of changing the volume. Likewise ArrowLeft/ArrowRight after a seek bar click now seek ±10s through the shortcut rather than stepping the range natively.
potential_unspecified_behavior.reason: Clicking the volume slider and then pressing ArrowUp to raise the volume a little more makes the video jump 60 seconds forward. The user notices and can press ArrowDown to undo it.

regression_risks: Keyboard fine-tuning after a mouse click on the volume or seek slider now runs the global seek shortcuts instead of the native range step (ShortcutsProvider.tsx:74-79, useVideoShortcuts.ts:28-63).
A volume drag released outside the slider may leave focus on it in some engines, which would bring back the bar-held-on-screen symptom (CR-2).
test_coverage: controls-autohide-focus-desktop.spec.ts covers a button click, a seek bar click and a volume slider click, each followed by a key press. It does not cover a drag released outside either slider.
No test checks what arrow keys do after a pointer click on the volume slider.
not_verified: Whether Chromium, Firefox and WebKit deliver pointerup to a native range input when a thumb drag is released outside it; no browser could be run.
Whether blur() resets the sequential focus navigation starting point in any engine (unspecified entry 0).
Unit tests and the e2e suite were not run.
